1) strain rate measurements using stake rosette systems; 2) determination of absolute velocities by utilizing geodetic positioning systems; 3) surface elevation determination; 4) measurements of surface accumulation using both stake systems and shallow cores; and 5) determination of 10-m temperatures. Thermal probes capable of measuring temperature and strain as a function of depth may be available for use at points along the flowline. In the borehole, time-dependent temperature and deformation studies will be conducted.
As part of the surface glaciology program, snow cores of about 10-m length will be collected at as many sites as possible. These cores will provide some information regarding accumulation rates on the ice shelf, but more important, they will provide materials for a study of the possible geographic variation in oxygen-isotope ratios.
The glaciological studies will supply information sufficient to calculate a bottom melting profile, investigate the dynamics of ice shelves along a flowline, calculate particle paths through the ice shelf, and investigate the history of the Ross Ice Shelf through the relatively recent past. The temperature-time relationships will bear directly on the question of surges of the West Antarctic ice sheet and whether or not the Ross Ice Shelf is in a steady-state condition.
